_doc: T-3645: every building card's opening line, as the floating card and Inspect's Overview show it (tools/reading_leads.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the line's own words, since many buildings share a composed line. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the line does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel readings) is left out.

8-10: A small camp of Potawatomi families who came to trade. It was on the south side of the river, where the creek runs in. It stood all through 1812. It is still being checked.
One of the two houses that Whistler drew in 1808, where the river splits in two. It stands here in 1812.

The farm cabin at Lee's Place in 1812. It was built again to match an old picture. On the river side it has three doors and six windows. The chimney is at one front corner. There is a shed of boards out back. The logs are painted white, and the roof is dark.
11-13: The farm cabin at Lee's Place in 1812, built again to match the old picture. Facing the river it has three doors and six windows. The chimney stands at the front corner of one end. A board shed leans on the back. The logs are whitewashed, and the roof is dark.
14-15: The farm cabin at Lee's Place in 1812, rebuilt to match the plate. The river front has three doors and six windows, with the chimney at the front corner of the upstream end. A plank lean-to stands behind it. The logs are whitewashed and the roof is darkened.

8-10: The fence around the field at Lee's Place in 1812.

The haystacks at Lee's Place in 1812. They stand across the river from the cabin. The owner said they looked like smooth, pale domes. So they were made again. Now they are lumpy, as if piled up by hand. Bits of hay stick out. Hay is stamped flat at the bottom. Each stack has its own shape. Some are fresh. Some have sunk down. Cows have eaten from some, and some have been cut.
11-13: The haystacks at Lee's Place in 1812, on the bank across from the cabin. The owner said they looked like smooth, pale domes, so they were made again. Now each is lumpy, as if pitched by hand, with wisps of hay sticking out and hay trampled at the foot. Each has its own shape: freshly piled, settled, eaten by the cattle, or cut from.
14-15: The haystacks at Lee's Place in 1812, on the bank across from the cabin. They were rebuilt after the owner reported that they looked like smooth, pale domes. Now each one is lumpy and hand-pitched, with wisps of hay standing out and trodden hay at its foot. Each has a shape of its own: freshly pitched, settled, fed on by the cattle, or cut from.

8-10: One of the three houses that Whistler drew in January 1808. They stood across the river, west of Kinzie's house. This one stands here in 1812.
The bake house at the Kinzie place, where bread was baked.
The house at the Kinzie place where people stayed and slept.
The stable at the Kinzie place, where the horses were kept. A book called Wau-Bun says it stood behind the house.
11-13: The stable at the Kinzie place. It is one of the buildings that the book Wau-Bun names behind the house.

8-10: The last of the three houses that Whistler drew in January 1808, across the river west of Kinzie's. It is the one closest to Kinzie's. In 1812 it is the home of Antoine Ouilmette.
It was a log wall around an army fort.
It was a small brick building where gunpowder was kept. It was one floor high.
It was a log house two floors high. The man in charge of the fort lived here.
11-13: It was a two-story log house for the fort's commanding officer.

8-10: It was a log house two floors high. The fort's officers lived here.
